problem: Learned navigation agents (UNREAL, CMP) had been compared almost only against other learned baselines, not against classical mapper/localizer/planner pipelines. High-level metrics such as SR and SPL also hide why and how agents fail, and the difficulty of the virtual environments was never characterized.
motivation: It is unclear whether deep learning actually beats hand-engineered pipelines, and where each is strong or weak. The answer would guide agent design and the design of test environments. The authors therefore build strong classical agents, define diagnostic metrics (collision, thrashing, exploitation, noise robustness) and environment metrics (ambiguity, complexity).
key_idea: Build strong hand-coded classical navigation agents (ICP localizer, occupancy mapper, A* planner, controller) for MINOS and S3DIS, beat the learned agents with them, and use diagnostic metrics to show what learning does and does not do well.
insight: Classical agents win on overall success because of far better collision avoidance and memory management: short-term thrashing is ~0-2% vs 21-66% for the learned agents, and collision frequency is 5.7% vs 66.1% for UNREAL. Learned agents win on robustness to noisy perception, where UNREAL with FCRN depth beats the classical agent (40.8 vs 11.4 SR on small houses), and on exploiting regularities under ambiguity (SPL-ambiguity correlation +0.13 for UNREAL vs -0.45 for classical). Classical failures come from noise propagating from the mapper and localizer into the planner and controller, which suggests hybrid designs.
method: Localizer: Libpointmatcher ICP (point-to-plane, KD-tree matcher, three runs with different features and 2D/3D inputs), with a consistency check against goal-relative geometry (0.2 m threshold), fallback to median action-outcome priors, and translation fine-tuning. In S3DIS, ground-truth pose is given.

Mapper: an analytic mapper back-projects depth to a 3D point cloud, thresholds height into obstacle/free, and updates a 2D occupancy grid (free discounts by 0.9, obstacle adds 0.5/d). A collision mapper marks cells as obstacles when a move has an unexpected outcome. S3DIS uses two binary maps, one per traversal direction.
Planner: converts the occupancy map to an 8-connected graph, with edge weight = 2000*cell occupancy + step cost (1 or 1.4), and runs weighted A* to produce waypoints.
Controller: picks the farthest straight-line-reachable waypoint as sub-goal in MINOS (continuous) or the closest waypoint in S3DIS (discrete), then moves forward if aligned and otherwise turns.
Diagnostic metrics: collision frequency, short-term thrashing Th_s, long-term thrashing Th_l, and exploitation M_e (unique 3D bins observed per unit of distance-to-goal reduction).
Noise tests: Gaussian depth noise at different levels, and depth estimated from RGB by FCRN trained on 70k MINOS images.

Environment metrics: ambiguity score (median steps of an idealized frontier-sampling 2D Monte Carlo agent divided by optimal path length) and complexity (number of turns on the optimal path), each correlated with per-episode SPL.

setting.backbone: Hand-coded classical pipeline (ICP + occupancy mapping + A* + controller); baselines are UNREAL (CNN-LSTM, RL) and CMP (pretrained, imitation)
setting.training_data: none for the classical agent (hand-coded; ICP fallback priors are medians from training data). UNREAL is retrained on MINOS train episodes for up to 13.2M steps; CMP uses the pretrained S3DIS model.
setting.observation: depth image plus goal distance/direction relative to view in MINOS; depth plus absolute pose and goal location in S3DIS
setting.action_space: MINOS: forward 0.2 m / turn ±7.2°; S3DIS: forward 0.8 m / turn ±90° / stay
setting.privileged: S3DIS: ground-truth pose given as part of the task. MINOS: none (a Classical-GT variant with GT localization is reported for reference only).

numbers_note: The paper does not explicitly name the split for the main tables (MINOS test episodes are presumably used); the diagnostic analyses use validation episodes. Noise robustness results are partly given only in a figure (Fig. all_gauss_noise). The paper's benchmarks are not in the canonical list, hence 'other:'.
results: The classical agent beats UNREAL on MINOS (SR 84.3 vs 50.5 small, 77.9 vs 20.2 medium) and beats CMP on S3DIS in 7 of 8 metrics (e.g. 70.0 vs 66.3 and 93.6 vs 78.5 SR on the 64-step task). Learned agents are worse at collision avoidance and thrashing but much more robust to depth noise and better at ambiguity.
limitations: The classical agents are hand-tuned separately for each environment and rely on ICP plus GT pose in S3DIS; comparisons cover only two simulators and two learned baselines (UNREAL, CMP).
UNREAL is reported as the best of five runs, and the paper suspects the previously reported MINOS numbers came from trivial episodes; the paper gives no significance analysis.
The correlation-based ambiguity and complexity analysis is coarse, with weak coefficients.
